title: Affordable housing targets and HART Hub launch
subtitle: Langs Drive rebuild loan, supervised consumption site closure, and improved paramedic response and ambulance offload times.
overview: The committee recommended that Council approve a revised Building Better Futures framework for 2025 to 2030, contingent on federal and provincial funding {{vote:m1}}. Staff reported that the first five-year target was met and set a new goal of 3,500 affordable homes created or preserved, with 60% aimed at very-low-to-low-income households. Preserving existing affordable housing is a new focus.

It also recommended a federal loan agreement for rebuilding Waterloo Region Housing's 589 Langs Drive in Cambridge {{vote:m2}}. The loan is secured against debentures, which gives the Region access to favourable federal terms. Tenants are being relocated and will have first right to return, and a youth centre is planned on site.

The committee received reports for information on the closure of the Kitchener consumption and treatment site on March 31 and the start of the HART Hub, which is not in a single location. Councillors raised concerns about the scale of the hub's services compared with community need. It also received two paramedic reports showing faster response times, lower ambulance offload delays and lower unit utilization in 2024. These items had no motions. All recommendations go to Council for a final decision.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council approve the revised framework as the Region's direction for creating and protecting affordable and non-market housing from 2025 to 2030, contingent on federal and provincial funding {{vote:m1}}.

The committee recommended authorizing a loan agreement with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the Cambridge housing rebuild, with senior staff authorized to sign the loan and related documents {{vote:m2}}.

debate: On housing, staff said the best measure of need is core housing need, meaning households paying over 30% of income on housing, which affects about 20,000 people in the region. They said the best place to invest is between supportive and affordable rental housing, and that the Region balances building new units with rent supplements in existing private and non-profit rentals.

A councillor asked about a municipal right of first refusal to buy properties for sale. Staff said it would need provincial legislation, that they do not know whether the province is open to it, and that they may pursue advocacy.

On rent-geared-to-income housing, a councillor relayed tenant concerns that rent rises when income rises. Staff said provincial rules set the calculation, rent is capped at 30% of income, the Region cannot require tenants to move, and it can offer incentives such as a home ownership program.

Several councillors said the HART Hub's 12 transitional beds and funding fall far short of need and do not replace supervised consumption. They raised long wait lists for supportive housing and treatment and the risk of overdoses during the gap after the March 31 closure. Staff and partners agreed need exceeds resources and said the province sets what it funds. They described mitigation steps, no expected wait list for the hub, and the aim of building evidence to seek more funding.

On paramedics, staff attributed improved response times to council investment and a drop in ambulance offload delays, helped by hospital leadership. They noted that response times are judged against a patient's acuity assessed on arrival, which dispatchers cannot know in advance, and said a new dispatch system should improve this. Alternative-destination clinics have not progressed, and ambulance purchases may face tariff cost impacts.
